text.content: Why state management matters in multi-step systems

rich_text.plain_text: Why state management matters in multi-step systems

text.content: In a single-agent, single-turn system, state is trivial. The agent receives input, produces output, and the run is complete. There is no position to track. But as soon as a system has multiple steps, multiple agents, or the possibility of interruption, state becomes a coordination surface.

text.content: Duplicate execution.

text.content: If a run is interrupted after the Classifier has executed but before the result is written to Flow State, and the system retries from the beginning, the Classifier runs again. Depending on the model's temperature and the input phrasing, it might produce a different classification the second time. The system now routes to a different specialist — for the same query, in the same session — without any record that the first classification happened.

text.content: Summary

rich_text.plain_text: Summary

text.content: State is the position of an execution in progress; what has completed, what the intermediate results are, and what the next step is waiting for. It is distinct from memory, which tracks what an agent knows from past interactions. The two interact, but confusing them produces systems that remember the past correctly and lose track of the present run.

It is distinct from memory, which tracks what an agent knows from past interactions. The two interact, but confusing them produces systems that remember the past correctly and lose track of the present run.

text.content: In Flowise, Flow State is the primary state surface: shared across the canvas, session-scoped, and structured. It is not automatic. What gets written to Flow State, when, and by which node are all design decisions. The failure modes that appear when those decisions are left unclear are the motivation for making them explicit.
